title: Drinking with the moon
hookLine: Li Bai drinks alone and invites the moon and his shadow to make three
tomorrow: a country falls. what does Du Fu see still standing?

cards: Table for one. Some people dread saying it out loud, as if it were a confession. Li Bai sits among the flowers with a jug of wine and no friend near.
So he raises his cup and invites the bright moon. With his shadow, that makes three.

teach.h: CAN YOU BE ALONE, NOT LONELY?
teach.b: The question is old: can you be alone without being lonely? Li Bai answers in steps. First, honesty: the moon doesn't drink, and the shadow only copies him.
Then play: he sings and the moon lingers; he dances and his shadow sprawls across the ground.
Then the ending: he and his two guests swear a friendship beyond ordinary feeling, and agree to meet again far off in the Milky Way.
Readers hear in that ending the Daoist ideal from the Zhuangzi: xiaoyao you, free and easy wandering, a self so at home in the whole of things that the moon counts as company.
So the answer, read this way: solitude isn't empty when you're at ease with the world that's already there. Now a neighbor, the Christian monks of the Egyptian desert.

teach.h: ABBA MOSES: SIT IN YOUR CELL.
teach.b: A brother came to Abba Moses asking for a word, and Moses told him, in effect: go, sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything. Shared: being alone can teach you, if you stay.
Honestly different: the desert monk stays alone to pray to God and face himself; Li Bai stays with a cup, the moon and play. One is a cell, one is a garden.

how: Daoist writers prize ease and free wandering, and Li Bai's moon poem is read in that light. Christian monastics, from the desert onward, keep solitude in a cell for prayer.

games.q: what does “drinking with the moon” mean?
o: a poem warning young men against drinking at night
a harvest toast to the full moon with the whole village
Li Bai's party for one, with the moon and his shadow as guests

games.q: two kinds of solitude: tap the pairs.
p: raised his cup to invite the moon
the third guest at the party
sit in your cell; it will teach you

s: Li Bai's poem is about the misery of drinking alone
he turns solitude into a party of three, and ends hoping to wander with the moon.
Abba Moses told a brother his cell would teach him everything
a desert saying: go, sit in your cell.
Li Bai and the desert monks are alone for the same reason
shared: solitude can teach. different: the monk prays to God; Li Bai plays with the moon.

games.q: since his friend died, your grandfather eats dinner alone and says he's fine. your aunt says it's sad. what fits today?
o: he may be at ease, like Li Bai with the moon; ask him, don't assume.
your aunt is right; anyone who eats alone is lonely.
being alone is only good if you spend it praying.
games.why: Li Bai finds company in the moon, Abba Moses finds a teacher in the cell. neither calls being alone sad by default.

practice: Sit as your own company. Close your eyes and notice who's here: the breath, the body, the sounds of the room, maybe your shadow on the floor. Treat them as guests, not as nothing.
If a lonely thought arrives, let it pull up a chair too.

wordCard.voice: Drinking with the moon: Li Bai's party of three, made from one man, the moon and his shadow.

orig.s: 舉杯邀明月 對影成三人
orig.say: jyoo bay yow ming yweh, dway ying chung sahn ren
orig.note: Chinese: I raise my cup to invite the bright moon; with my shadow we make three. Li Bai.

carryVoice: A line to keep: the moon and my shadow, alone and still in company. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Li Bai, Drinking Alone under the Moon (Yue xia du zhuo), poem 1
sources.q: 花間一壺酒，獨酌無相親。舉杯邀明月，對影成三人。
